## My Reasoning

I've been farming this land in Quzhou my whole life. At 68, I know exactly what this ground can do and what it demands. The North China Plain — my land — runs on winter wheat and summer maize. That double rotation is what I know, what the market pays for, and what our soils and water infrastructure are set up to support. I'm not going to experiment at my age with cash crops or vegetables on any serious scale. The wheat is already in the ground from last October. It's April now, so I'm entering the critical jointing-to-filling window for the wheat, then I'll roll directly into maize after June harvest.

I have 10 mu under cultivation — a size I can still manage with my son coming back at harvest. I planted **Kenong 199** wheat last autumn, an improved variety approved for Hebei that does well on our loam soils. I applied base fertilizer at sowing already. Now I'll top-dress nitrogen at jointing stage and irrigate twice: once now at jointing, once at grain filling. Quzhou's water table has been dropping for years — I was part of an agricultural water-saving trial years back and I took those lessons seriously. Two irrigations is enough if I time them right. I'll do the "一喷三防" (one spray, three protections) in May — fungicide, insecticide, and foliar nutrient combined — that's been standard practice here for years and it works.

For summer maize I'll plant **Xianyu 335** hybrid immediately after wheat harvest, using rotary tillage to turn the stubble fast. Summer rains usually cover most of what maize needs; I'll irrigate once at silking if July is dry. One post-emergence herbicide application, that's it. Nitrogen goes in two splits — base at planting, topdress at V6-V8. I keep phosphorus and potassium moderate; soil tests I've had done show we don't need to push those.

I keep my inputs measured. I've seen neighbors over-fertilize and watch their costs eat the profit. With grain prices where they are, margin comes from discipline, not yield maximization.
